To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

homesigner children use a variety of gesture types to communicate about objects and actions, that these gestures are combined to create multigesture constituents, and that these constituents serve the same functions as single gestures.

deaf homesigners use multigesture nominal units to refer to entities, that these multigesture units function as nominal constituents, that these nominal constituents are used in a syntactic structure, and that these syntactic structures are used to refer to entities in discourse.

homesigners build hierarchical structures in their self-created communication system by combining gestures into nominal constituents that function as units in the same way as do demonstrative gestures and nouns in spoken languages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of hierarchical constituent structure in the absence of a conventional language.
the development of a hierarchical structure in the homesign system, a self-created communication system that does not have a conventional model.
the emergence of a new language in the absence of a conventional language model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children who do not have access to a conventional language nevertheless build hierarchical structures in a self-created communication system.
